query_full: How frequently is foreign press barred or allowed in war zones? (Yes, this is motivated by the question about press access to Gaza, but don't read support, or criticism, for that question in this one. Merely curiosity about how much we can expect free press access in conflict zones). To give some context of my understanding coming into this question: During the Vietnam War, the US, consciously or not, experimented with press freedom in a war zone. This was largely seen to have been a mistake from the US PoV, whether or not one agreed with war itself . From burning napalm on a child, to a self-immolating monk, to a spot execution of a bound communist sympathizer, a number of instantly-recognizable photos contributed in driving down US domestic support for the war. I kinda recall people stating that that access had been a) unusual and b) mismanaged. With the unusual aspect relevant to my question here. By Gulf War 1, the US had learned its lesson and the press coverage about press coverage was fascinated by the solution found: embedded journalists . Who were vetted, and controlled by, the Pentagon. So, yes, there was access. But, no, it wasn't free access. And, if I recall correctly, no one was much surprised or outraged, just a bit cynical about the press freedom quotient to be expected. In the Ukraine war, the press does have access to the Ukraine side of things. But even people highly sympathetic to Ukraine can understand that Ukraine has a vested interest in presenting its plight on the world stage. Free press access is of benefit to Ukraine, which is not doubt a huge part of the reasons it is allowed. On the Russian side of things, no, I don't think there is free access to foreign journalists to the occupied regions. They do conduct tours , of sorts, mostly with picked Western "journalists" of dubious quality. India has found it expedient at times to bar foreign press in Kashmir for months at a time. RSF in 2020 : "The Kashmir Valley, from which foreign reporters had already been barred for several months" Yes, there are plenty of counterinsurgency conflicts - presumably what Gaza is supposed to be at this point - where press is allowed, under various levels of control, by the official government. But in many cases, the "coverage of the coverage" also points out the reason: the government wants to appear strong and in control and a press blackout would give the opposite impression. Keep that in mind when looking at historical access to Gaza - just because it was allowed at one time doesn't mean the same calculation about the cost/benefit applies nowadays, from the Israeli side. Yes, at times Israel has allowed foreign press into Gaza, under highly controlled conditions, for example to show tunnels under hospitals. This is akin to Gulf War 1 embedded reporters and isn't generally seen as free press access. Guerrillas, rebels and sometimes even terrorists often explicitly covet coverage, consider press access a tool in their struggle and therefore allow it. But, like Ukraine, one should be under no illusion about why this is allowed, regardless of where one's sympathy lies. So, on balance is foreign press access the norm, or the exception, in conflict zones, on the government side? Especially by democracies, rather than authoritarian regimes. p.s. At the risk of stating the obvious, the press itself will almost always insist on press freedom. This question isn't about what the press thinks, nor whether public opinion thinks that the press should be allowed or not. It is concerned with what is normative/customary with regards to foreign press access in war zones. p.p.s. Be cautious about survivor bias here. Merely citing all the conflict coverage you can recall doesn't tell us much about the cases where it wasn't allowed. p.p.p.s. It was already in the comments, but it seems to have been missed: while it is motivated by the Gaza situation this question is explicitly not about Gaza : we already know the foreign press is barred there.
query_title: How frequently is foreign press barred or allowed in war zones?

The actual Enumeration shall be made ... within every subsequent Term of ten Years, in such Manner as they shall by Law direct." So big states (w.r.t. population) get more representatives than do small states. The Constitution does not spell out how many total representatives there are in the House nor exactly the manner that the apportionment shall determine how many each state gets. It's just that every 10 years, we must have a Census for which the primary Constitutional purpose is to determine how the U.S. House of Representatives is apportioned among the now 50 U.S. states. The data from the Census gets used in a variety of ways and purposes, but this is the original primary purpose of the U.S. Decennial Census. It's a big deal. (I would presume, in the European Union, that they have the same issue, but maybe settle the issue differently .) So then, the specific number of U.S. representatives and the specific manner of proportionately distributing their seats to the various states is a matter of federal law (one notch lower than the Constitution) and is spelled out in U.S.C. Title 2 . Well, not really completely spelled out, hence this question. Okay, I know and understand what "the method known as the method of equal proportions" is. It's also known as the Huntington-Hill Method and is referred to as "the method known as the method of equal proportions" in §2a and §2b of U.S.C. Title 2 . There is also some useful history to read but I want to see the actual document in law that spells it out. Even if it was a report transmitted to Congress circa 1941, I would like to see what a federal judge would be saying that "this is what the law is" and I cannot find that.
